issues.legal_issue: An order in an appeal concerning one taxpayer permits an assessment of another taxpayer beyond the ordinary limitation period only if it contains a necessary finding about that other taxpayer’s taxability or an express, authorized direction requiring that assessment.
material_facts: In appeals concerning a partnership firm’s assessments, the appellate authority found that the firm did not own the properties because the construction costs had been debited to the individual co-owners’ accounts.

The appellate authority did not determine that the excess construction costs represented the individual co-owners’ taxable income; that would have required a separate inquiry and an opportunity for them to be heard.
The appellate authority observed that the tax officer was free to take action against the co-owners, leaving it to the officer’s option whether to do so.

The tax officer later assessed the excess construction costs as income of the individuals, and the assessments were upheld on the basis that the earlier order engaged the extended limitation provision.
issues.conclusion: The earlier order contained neither a finding nor a direction within the meaning of section 153(3)(ii) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, and that provision did not apply to the individual assessments. The appeals were allowed and the matter was remanded to the High Court to address the separate question concerning section 147(a).
issues.legal_principle: Under section 153(3)(ii), a finding must be necessary for disposing of the particular case concerning the particular taxpayer and assessment year; an incidental finding about another taxpayer is insufficient. A finding about another taxpayer may be necessary where income can belong only to one of two persons and deciding ownership as to one determines the other’s liability. A direction must be express, necessary to dispose of the case, and within the authority’s power; a statement that an officer is free to act is not a direction because it requires no positive compliance. Explanation 3 requires an opportunity to be heard before a finding that an amount is another person’s income. Section 153(3)(ii) only removes a limitation bar and does not enlarge jurisdiction. The Court relied on Income Tax Officer, A-Ward, Sitapur v. Murlidhar Bhagwan Das and N. Kt. Sivalingam Chettiar v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras, and distinguished Commissioner of Income-tax, Andhra Pradesh v. Vadde Pullaiah & Co.

rule.if: firm_assessment_appeal and only_firm_ownership_determined and individual_income_not_determined_after_hearing and action_left_optional

predicates.firm_assessment_appeal: The earlier proceeding was an appeal concerning the assessment of a business entity rather than the later individual assessments.
predicates.only_firm_ownership_determined: The appellate authority determined only that the business entity did not own the property, without determining that the excess expenditure was another person’s taxable income.
predicates.individual_income_not_determined_after_h: The individual’s taxability of the amount was not determined after an inquiry in which that individual had an opportunity to be heard.
predicates.action_left_optional: The earlier order left it to the tax officer’s choice whether to take action against the individuals.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a business entity, determines only that the entity did not own property, leaves the individuals’ taxability undetermined after a hearing, and makes any further action optional, the earlier order does not permit an individual assessment beyond the ordinary limitation period.
